characters: Teye: 11-year-old Ghanaian boy with a neat low haircut, wearing a bright yellow football jersey and blue shorts, holding a classic black-and-white football.
Akweley: 11-year-old Ghanaian girl with neat braided hair tied with blue ribbons, wearing a coral-orange top, khaki skirt and carrying a small field notebook.
Grandpa Nii: Warm elderly Ghanaian fisherman with silver-grey hair and beard, wearing a woven straw hat and indigo cotton shirt while mending a fishing net.
Madam Ofori: Kind Primary 5 teacher in a teal-and-gold Ghanaian print dress and spectacles.
Sena: Teye’s classmate living near the shoreline, wearing a green polo shirt.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, expressive Ghanaian-English storyteller voice (Kore) with clear classroom and coastal atmosphere
narrationPlan.pace: Steady, clear developing/fluent reader pace (about 115 words per minute)
notes: Emphasize the scientific caution around investigating local coastal causes.
Keep dialogue natural and distinct for Teye, Akweley, Grandpa Nii and Madam Ofori.

music: Gentle Atlantic Breeze Piano (soft, reflective coastal piano melody ducked beneath narration)
culturalNotes: Teye (Dangme), Akweley (Ga), Nii (Ga) and Sena (Ewe) reflect coastal communities along Ghana’s Greater Accra, Volta and Eastern shorelines.
Fishing nets, beach football and community centre meetings are everyday features of life in Ghanaian coastal towns.
reviewQuestions: Are all causes of coastal erosion presented carefully as requiring local investigation rather than assuming a single cause?
Does the story clearly reject dumping plastic and old tyres on the beach as polluting and ineffective?

pages.brief: 3D animated scene on a sunny Ghanaian sandy beach. 11-year-old Teye in a yellow football jersey holding a football and 11-year-old Akweley in a coral top look surprised at wooden goalposts lying in wet sand touched by foaming ocean waves. Nearby, Grandpa Nii in a straw hat and indigo shirt sits mending a fishing net.
pages.narration: Open with lively curiosity, surprise on Teye’s question, and thoughtful warmth from Grandpa Nii.

pages.brief: 3D animated close-up scene by the beach veranda. Grandpa Nii holds an open carved wooden box and shows an old sepia-toned photograph of wide sandy beach and coconut palms to Teye and Akweley, who compare the photo with the closer ocean waves behind them.
pages.narration: Read Grandpa Nii’s explanation calmly and clearly, emphasizing the phrase "coastal erosion".

pages.brief: 3D animated bright Ghanaian classroom. Madam Ofori in a teal-and-gold print dress and spectacles gently tilts water in a clear shallow tray half-filled with sloped beach sand, showing sand grains shifting as Teye raises his hand and Akweley takes notes.
pages.narration: Clear, engaging teacher tone during the tray experiment, highlighting scientific caution.

pages.brief: 3D animated afternoon scene in a Ghanaian coastal village. Teye and his classmate Sena watch empathetically as Sena’s mother carries household boxes away from a compound wall near the sandy shoreline, with ocean waves visible in the background.
pages.narration: Gentle, empathetic tone showing Teye’s growing understanding of how erosion affects real families.

pages.brief: 3D animated schoolyard discussion. Akweley holds up her hand thoughtfully while speaking to classmates, and Madam Ofori points to an educational chart illustrating healthy coastal mangroves and engineered sea defences.
pages.narration: Firm, thoughtful voice for Akweley and Madam Ofori explaining why rubbish is not a coastal defence.

pages.brief: 3D animated classroom scene. Teye and Akweley stand beside a project board showing old and new shoreline photos and interview notes while a visiting Ghanaian female coastal scientist in field attire and a lanyard smiles and explains coastal monitoring instruments.
pages.narration: Encourage a sense of discovery and respect for long-term scientific measurement.

pages.brief: 3D animated community centre meeting in Ghana. Teye stands bravely beside Akweley in front of a display of shoreline photographs, speaking to an attentive audience of parents, Grandpa Nii, fishers, engineers and local officials who applaud warmly.
pages.narration: Sincere, courageous tone as Teye speaks to the community, building to warm applause.

pages.brief: 3D animated golden sunset scene overlooking the Ghanaian coast from a safe grassy rise. Teye holding his football, Grandpa Nii in his straw hat, and Akweley holding her notebook laugh warmly together as golden sunlight shimmers on the gentle ocean waves.
pages.narration: Warm, hopeful and joyful ending as Teye and Akweley share their dreams.

teacherGuide.overview: Introduce erosion and sediment movement with a supervised tray demonstration. Explain that coastal change has multiple causes and that local evidence matters. Do not take children near unstable cliffs, dangerous surf or eroding structures.
learningGoals: Explain that coastal erosion is the wearing away or removal of material from a coast by waves, currents and water movement.
Identify factors that can contribute to coastal change, including waves, currents, storms and rising sea level, while recognising the need for local investigation.
Evaluate why dumping rubbish on the beach is harmful and why coastal protection requires scientific assessment and community planning.

beforeReading: Ask learners whether they have ever seen water move sand or soil during heavy rain or at the beach.
Preview the title "The Sea That Came Closer" and ask what might happen if the shoreline moves toward a community.
whileReading: Pause at Page 1 and Page 3 for the embedded quick questions on why Teye was surprised and what the tray experiment demonstrated.
On Page 5, discuss why Akweley and Madam Ofori rejected the idea of piling plastic bags and tyres on the beach.
afterReading: Guide learners through the five end-of-story tasks: naming contributors to coastal change, defining coastal erosion, explaining why rubbish dumping fails, comparing shoreline photos carefully, and designing a "Protect Our Coast" poster.
discussion: Why did Madam Ofori say we must investigate local conditions before deciding what causes changes at a particular beach?
How did Teye, Akweley, parents, fishers, engineers and officials work together at the community meeting?
reflection: What environmental change have you noticed in your own community, and how could you investigate it safely with adult guidance?

mathsExtension.task: Suppose a safe observation marker is placed 35 metres from the high-water line, and after a year of measurements the high-water line is 32 metres from the marker. How many metres closer did the high-water line move that year?

support: Use the classroom sand-and-water tray demonstration before reading so learners can see sediment movement firsthand.
stretch: Have learners write three interview questions they would ask a coastal engineer or local elder about how the environment has changed over time.

culturalNotes: Coastal fishing and beach football are central to community life in towns along Ghana’s coast.
localiseThis: For inland schools, connect the tray demonstration to soil erosion along riverbanks, school compounds or gullies after heavy rainfall.

whatWeKnow: Waves, currents, storms and sea-level changes transport sediment and reshape coastlines through erosion and deposition.
Dumping plastic waste and old tyres pollutes marine ecosystems and does not provide engineered coastal protection.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Coastal scientists and engineers continuously monitor how local currents, sediment supply and long-term sea-level trends interact at specific beaches.

investigation.title: Supervised Classroom Sand-and-Water Tray Demonstration
materials: A shallow plastic or metal tray
steps: Shape clean sand at one end of the shallow tray to model a gentle beach slope.
Pour water carefully into the other end of the tray.
Gently tilt or wave a ruler in the water and observe how grains of sand shift and move.
investigation.whatToNotice: Moving water picks up and transports sand grains (sediment), changing the shape of the model shoreline.
investigation.safetyNote: Conduct inside the classroom under teacher supervision. Never take children near unstable cliffs, dangerous surf or eroding coastal structures.

factCheck.claim: Waves, currents, storms and changes in sea level can affect coastlines, and local conditions must be investigated.
factCheck.explanation: Coastal morphodynamics depend on wave energy, longshore currents, sediment supply, human activities and relative sea-level change.
factCheck.reference: IPCC AR6 Working Group I & II Reports on Coastal Systems; EPA Ghana Coastal Zone Management guidelines
